title: Sex Differences in Sleep Architecture in Persons with Obstructive Sleep Apnea – Data from the Sleep Heart Health Study
journal: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine

sections.abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title> <jats:p>Introduction: Sex-related differences in the prevalence and clinical manifestations of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) have been well-documented, with men experiencing higher prevalence and distinct symptomatology compared to women. However, it remains unclear whether sleep architecture differs between men and women at equivalent levels of OSA severity in the absence of confounding medical conditions. Thus, this study aimed to examine sex differences in sleep structure among adults with OSA, independent of comorbidities. Methods: Data from the Sleep Heart Health Study were used to identify a cohort of men and women with moderate-to-severe OSA (Apnea-Hypopnea Index ≥ 15 events/hr based on CMS criteria) but without medical comorbidities, including angina, myocardial infarction, heart failure, coronary artery bypass grafting, percutaneous transluminal coronary angioplasty, stroke, type 2 diabetes, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Sleep architecture variables, including sleep stages (N1, N2, slow-wave sleep, and REM sleep) and arousal frequency, were assessed using overnight home polysomnography data. Quantile regression models were applied to examine sex differences in sleep architecture. Results: Men had significantly higher Stage 1 sleep (Δ: 2.59, p=0.007), indicating a greater proportion of light sleep compared to women. Conversely, men demonstrated lower percentages of slow-wave sleep (Δ: -7.35, p=0.001) and REM sleep (Δ: -3.70, p=0.036) compared to women. These findings suggest distinct patterns in sleep architecture between men and women with OSA, independent of confounding medical conditions. Conclusion: This study demonstrates significant sex differences in sleep architecture among adults with moderate-to-severe OSA, with men exhibiting worse objective parameters of sleep architecture relative to women. These differences may have implications for understanding sex-specific pathophysiological mechanisms in OSA and tailoring clinical interventions to address sex-based variations in sleep patterns. Further research is needed to explore the clinical significance of these architectural differences and their potential impact on the health outcomes associated with OSA in men and women.</jats:p>
